of the soil.
As a man who works with his hands, Mr Cunliffe will appreciate this week’s
announcement of $20 million in the Budget fo r 6,000 more apprenticeships, which will
give eligible apprentices or trainees an opportunity to apply for a $1,000 subsidy
towards the costs of tools and off-job course costs, or $2,000 for those in priority trades.
So what we have with Mr Cunliffe is a very, very strange person, and Wallace Chapman
is not the only person to have identified this . He is always secretive and always darting
around the edges of the truth. We have the se cret trusts, we have those extraordinary
statements about the whaling case, which was a triumph for this country, and he denied
that we were there. As Sunday’s radio interv iew showed, he is so adept at being tricky
that when he has no one to deceive, he deceives  himself just to keep in practice. He is a
very, very odd fish indeed. When he talks about the stark contrasts in the next few
months, I will place the house on this fellow Ke y going head to head with Cunliffe and
crushing him.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I have some respect for the
Attorney-General, but a week out from the Budget, as we approach an election, I have
to say that that was a very lightweight speech. As we head into the election season, a
few weeks away from the Budget, you are going to hear less from the Labour Party
about the other side and more about the di fference that we are going to bring to New
Zealanders’ lives. Of course we  are still going to be exposi ng the cronyism that is rife
under this Government. I do not have time to go  into that any more today, other than to
say that it is the responsibility of the Opposition to hold the Government to account for
poor practice, in the interests of democracy.
I want to talk about why it is that our re visions to monetary policy struck a chord
with New Zealand. It is a topi c that is not particularly se xy, but it was well received by
New Zealanders because they are now seei ng the linkages between what the Labour
Party stands for and the lives that they live. They see that our policies are connected to
improving their lives in the way and in the ar eas that they worry about. They know that
despite the fact that New Zealand had low ge neral price inflation in the last quarter—
zero percent, excluding the increase in tax on  cigarettes—house price inflation is out of
control, particularly in Auckland, and that is why the Reserve Bank put up interest rates,
which, in turn, put up the exchange rate. Th ey know that there has been a 40 percent
increase in house prices in Aucklan d. The average is now $680,000. Homeownership
rates are at a 50-year low. That is one of the most important measures of rising
inequality under this Government.
New Zealanders know that because interest  rates went up because of poor housing
policy, it has meant that people have lost their jobs in the forest processing industry, that
we export too many raw logs, and that the problems of insecure work and of an
unemployment rate still at 6 percent are re lated to housing policy and monetary policy.
They know that the Government hides the lot of ordinary New Zealanders in its
averages. It says average wages have gone  up, when it knows that  45 percent of New
Zealanders did not get any wage increase la st year and that, even on average, the
average wage rate went up by only 1.6 percent, which is exactly the same as the
increase in inflation. They know that we ar e on to something and that we have got to
align the objectives of the Reserve Bank with our export sector.
We hear Steven Joyce coming in here and trying to minimise, trying to dissect down
to the littlest thing, and trying to reject the idea that we have actually got some pretty
comprehensive policies that work across the economy to reduce interest rates, to get our
interest rates down to lower levels, which are always higher than the rest of the world,
17578 General Debate 7 May 2014
and which jack up our exchange rate and mean that we have not covered the cost of our
imports in interest for 40 years. They know that those changes are complex but
important. They know that it is better to sa ve a bit more money than to pay it on
interest. They know that the Australians have done that and that is why the Australians
sustain higher income rates and lower intere st rates. That is why they like universal
KiwiSaver.
New Zealanders know that there are lots of other tools that the Reserve Bank has got,
like macro-prudential tools, that it could use differently. They know that a capital gains
tax, to tax speculators, not the family home, would take the heat out of the price of
houses, and would therefore have less lead fr om the Reserve Bank to jack up interest
rates. They know that we should restrict  foreign buyers buying existing homes. They
can build a new one; they cannot just buy an existing one, because that pushes up prices
to the detriment of New Zealanders and their children. They know that the same thing is
happening with farmland.
The Labour Party is determined—it is determined—to bring our interest rates back to
international norms. We have got a once in a life time opportunity, as we transition to
compulsory or universal KiwiSaver, to ge t saving rates up and in terest rates down, to
get people into their first home by helping them save for a deposit, and to help people in
our productive sector, because our excha nge rate will not be overvalued beyond its
fundamentals. What was the Government’s response? Bill English said that it is bad that
the exchange rate is too high, but it is bad if it settles at realistic levels. He said there is
nothing new in this, but no one has done it before.
On this side of the House we are determined to bring forward policies that will help
people have secure work, bett er-paid jobs, lower interest rates, more export earnings,
and better lives.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: That speech
made by David Parker really shows the problems that the Labour Party has. David
Parker is a very nice, pleasan t, naïve fellow, trying to expl ain where Labour is at with
economic policy. Frankly, none of that makes se nse to the person in the street. The fact
is that it was a whole lot of garbage. In economic terms David Parker is like the bloke at
the rugby club who still showers in his underpants. That is wher e he is at. He is totally
naïve and out of touch. He has got this policy thing that he is calling the “big tool”. The
problem is that no one out there in the real  world can understand what the heck he is
talking about. It is all academic mumbo-jumbo.  It is no wonder that  David Parker is not
an electorate MP, because, quite frankly, he has no connection with real people, just like
David Cunliffe, his leader, who makes out that he has been a guy who has sheared
sheep and done all this sort of stuff.

items.speaker: Hon Chris Tremain
items.text: He was a war hero.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Yeah, his grandad was a war hero or whatever.
Well, that was not true. In actual fact, David Cunliffe hides out in his Herne Bay
mansion pretending to be the New Lynn blue-collar man, and it just does not work.
I will tell you something ve ry interesting. I do not know  whether you listened to
Radio New Zealand National this morning, but Guyon Espiner asked Grant Robertson
whether he thought that his lead er should reveal the details of  his secret trust. I will tell
you what: Grant Robertson woul d not back up David Cunliffe . He would not back him
up. Grant Robertson was one of the 68 percen t of people in the Labour caucus who did
not want David Cunliffe as leader.
The problem they have is that the Labour Party leadership is now for sale. And who
have they sold it to? They have sold the leadership to the unions. Basically, 70 percent
of unions voted for David Cunliffe. Now th e Labour Party has to deliver on what the
unions want. That is a real problem because what the unions actually want is not what
7 May 2014 General Debate 17579
New Zealand wants. So these people, as Stev en Joyce has said, ha ve been caught up in
all sorts of distractions all week.
Meanwhile, National is delivering for New Zealanders. There is fantastic economic
growth. There is 3 to 4 percent growth in  GDP predicted over the coming year. There
were 68,000 jobs created over the past year. The balance of payments is extremely
healthy. Terms of trade are the best they have been for a long, long time. David Cunliffe
was going on about interest rates, but do you  know what they were under Labour in
2008? For a first mortgage they were 11 per cent. That party was crippling the average
Kiwi. So those guys do not have the record to stand on.
David Parker was also talking about overs eas investment and how he is going to do
this and that and that New Zealand is not for sale. Well, David Parker—their finance
spokesman—personally signed off much, much more land in his 5 years doing the job
than we have in our entire time in Government. So these guys talk one game in
Opposition but they are totally different in Government. We are just focusing on getting
on with the job. We are focused on health, education, the economy, and law and order—
the things that matter to New Zealanders.
Tony Ryall today announced $6.2 million for co chlea implants so that kids can hear.
That makes a real difference. Paula Benne tt announced that there was $10 million for
sexual violence counselling services in the Budge t. It is so important. The Christchurch
announcement was about paying $3,000 to get be neficiaries off their backsides and
down to Christchurch to work, develop a career, and add something to the economy. We
are tackling real problems.
Those guys over there are just making it up. We have not heard any policy from
Labour apart from the “big tool”. But do you know how bad it has got over there? It has
got so bad that Labour has had to prom ote Trevor Mallard to be its economic
development spokesman. Labour has now had to put Trevor—who is finished, whom
the New Zealand public hate—at No. 15 because the only guy there with any economic
clue, Shane Jones, has actually said: “I’m out  of here. I’m not going to be part of any
Labour-Green setup.” What did he say? He said that Labour and the Greens together
will not be promoting economic development. Shane Jones knows which way it is
going. Shane Jones knows that it makes sense to  come and work for the Government of
New Zealand, because we focus on what Ki wis care about. And when it comes to the
election, people are going to put all the rubbish—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Oravida.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Oh, that is David Clar k for Dunedin North. He
is the guy who says that he will ban Google fr om New Zealand. What an idiot. That is
the standard we have got. He is another “shower in his underp ants” bloke—the vicar
from Dunedin who thinks he can help run the economy. I tell you what: those people are
in trouble big time. We are delivering in health and education. We have the lowest
crime rate in 25 years. Kids are achieving at school, and the Polynesian community is
achieving. I can tell you what. Labour member s can say what they like, but the public
know which side their bread is buttered on.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: Yesterday the United States released its
national climate assessment report. Its main message is that climate change is not a
distant threat but a clear and present danger. To quote the report: “Climate change, once
considered an issue for a distant future, ha s moved firmly into the present. Americans
are noticing changes all around them. Summers  are longer and hotter, and periods of
extreme heat last longer than any … Amer ican has ever experi enced. Winters are
generally shorter and warmer. Rain come s in heavier downpours, though in many
regions there are longer dry spells in be tween.” This follows the latest UN Fifth
Assessment Report, which advances the same conclusions at the global level. “The
17580 General Debate 7 May 2014
debate over climate evidence is over.”, to quote one of the lead authors of the US report.
Except that there never really was a debate  over climate change—or at least there
should never have been.
Climate science is not a matter of subjectiv e political judgment. It involves natural
processes where the scientific method a pplies, with hypotheses and evidence self-
correcting to a higher level of confidence. The scientists sounded the alarm in 1988. The
international community formally identifie d the danger in 1992. It launched its first
response strategy in 1997. Then, in 2005, the then Opposition leader, John Key, advised
the world that he was scep tical of global warming. Coming to power in 2008 he began
weakening New Zealand’s response strate gy, assisted by a cohort of troglodytes
determined to undermine any purposeful climate policy.
New Zealanders would be able  to report similar experience s with climate change as
those of the Americans—recent storms and fl oods, droughts and fires, and sea level rise
that is already occurring. But there is no re port. The Government has no interest. Last
sitting week an eminent group presented a petition to Parliament urging the Government
to undertake a risk assessment of New Z ealand. Not one National MP was on hand to
receive the petition. The petitioners, above a ll, appealed for a cross-party accord on
climate change. An hour late r I highlighted the petition in general debate. Not one
National MP acknowledged the petition.
Judith Collins spoke about the economy, law and order, health, and welfare, just as
Jonathan Coleman has just now—pretty much  everything that matters to ordinary
Kiwis, as she put it, with exquisite ignorance of the petition that had just been tabled.
The ever-prescient David Be nnett contented himself with  the humble view that the
Green Party represents a vision that has gone. It represents, he said, a vision of the past.
Ian McKelvie enthused that  it was another great day for provincial New Zealand
because it was raining everywhere, except, he cried, the lower Rangit īkei. Significant
rain, he warned, again, with unwitting irony, will be needed very soon. And he was kind
enough to explain why “For those who do not  understand this …”, tupping will not be
as productive with less rain.
What has to occur to bring this ideological ly blind Government to its senses? During
the last dismantlement of the emissions tr ading scheme in this House I accused John
Key and Tim Groser of the moral crime of ecocide. I make that charge again today
because these leaders are w ilfully maintaining a respons e strategy that condemns New
Zealanders to a future that undermines our economy, including agriculture.

items.speaker: Last weekend the UN Secretary-General said this
items.text: “The planet is sending us clearly a
message that nature is now sick. We must  listen. That is why I am saying to world
leaders: ‘Don’t be on the losing side of history. Change is in the air. Solutions exist. The
race is on. It’s time to lead.’ ” John Key a nd Tim Groser are, in fact, leading on the
losing side. New Zealand’s net emissions are projected to triple between 1990 and 2030.
The rate of increase is higher than globa l emission projections. Global projections are
expected to breach the 2 degree threshold and land us in danger territory—somewhere
between 2.6 and 4.5 degrees. But if the world emitted at the rate New Zealand is
projected to, the global temper ature would rise by 5 to 7 degrees—truly catastrophic.
This is how New Zealand, under John Key, is doing its fair share. The man should be
ashamed of himself and his Government.

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I have a really good feeling about
the Budget. I have got a good f eeling about the Budge t because it is absolutely focused
on the things that matter most to New Zeal anders and their families. It is about
opportunity, it is about economic well-being, and it is about providing a good quality of
life for everyone.
7 May 2014 General Debate 17581
Firstly, and so importantly, we are moving back  into surplus. It is not a huge surplus
but we are on the way to ongoing surpluses and the opportunity to strengthen our
economy by paying down debt so that we can keep our interest rates down, as low as
possible, and put something aside for the next rainy day. It is so good to see our
economy growing. Now we have to lock down that growth so that everyone—our
families, our households, and our businesses— can benefit. Yes, we have all worked
pretty long and pretty hard and pretty sm art to get here, and we have managed to
survive really tough global economic times a nd survive them well, but now we have to
manage that economic growth equally as intellig ently so that we can continue to benefit
into the future. We want more jobs and we want better incomes, and the only way to get
those is by sticking to our very successful  economic management plan and focusing on
our Business Growth Agenda.
Canterbury and the Chri stchurch rebuild are a key focu s of this Government, and a
significant amount of the new Budget money is targeted at supporting our community—
firstly, supporting our very resilient but by now pretty tired and stressed families. The
Minister for Social Development, Paul a Bennett, has announced $13.5 million in
operational funding over the next 4 years to continue the Earthquake Support
Coordination Service. It is a great service.  It includes counselli ng and the Canterbury
0800 support phone line. I know of dozens of pe ople who have benefited from the free
counselling, and hundreds, maybe thousands, who have got support on that phone line.
This money will provide ongoing earthquake coordination to support 5,000 households
and about 250 new people every month to go through counselling services. It is
estimated that the 0800 number will handl e nearly 13,000 calls in the next year.
International research tells us that the third ye ar after a major disaster is often the worst.
It is very stressful for our families, so we really need and appreciate this support.
I am always very pleased to see the $20 million allocated for 6,000 new
apprenticeships and the incentives for beneficiar ies to come to Christchurch to take up
pre-arranged jobs. I am really pleased b ecause in the past adjournment I have had
several businesses talking to me about desperately needing more workers. I have spoken
to construction companies that have thanke d us for the apprenticeship reboot scheme,
and they say that it has been a real breakthrough for them and has increased the number
of apprenticeships that they can take up, and that is great for our young people.

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: Where are they going to live, Nicky?

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: Also, to the interest of Carol Beaumont, who questioned
earlier, I recently visited the Christchurch Polytechnic Institute of Technology women’s
trade training course and I met a fabul ous group of women—about 60 of them—who
are working hard and just itching to get out  and work on that rebuild. Although we are
getting through the repairs, we are only about 10 percent thr ough the construction
phase, so there is plenty of work for them once they have graduated.
Other businesses that I visited are also very short of staff. I met one that was short of
40 full-time semi-skilled workers. It wants to  continue to expand and this is what is
stopping it. It pays well, it is family friendl y, and it is flexible, but it still cannot get
enough employees. There was also a smaller company that was short of only a couple of
workers, but for that size of company it is crucial if they want to continue to grow.
There is work in Christchurch—all type s of work—and I welcome people who are
keen to come to our city and add to the rebuild and our city’s prosperity.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I think it is pertinent when we come to a Budget to
ask a really simple question. It is a que stion that I think we should ask every
Government when it is in office, and it is whom the Government is here for. When
judging a Government on a question like that, actions will always speak louder than
words or the rhetoric that we have had from that side of the House this afternoon. Let us
17582 General Debate 7 May 2014
look at the Government’s action. Let us look  at its record since it first came into
Government.
It may brush over this, but one of the firs t things that it did was reorder our tax
system so that tax cuts—significant ones—meant that 40 percent of what it redistributed
went to the top 10 percent of New Zealanders . When this Government claims that it is
moving back into surplus, we need to k eep in context that it is borrowing up to $10
million worth of interest a day in order to pay for tax cuts like that, which went to
people who just did not need them. That wa s the trade-off that the Government was
willing to make. At the same time, it cut things  like the training incentive allowance. It
scrapped adult and community education.  It has poured $40 million into private
schooling and established charter schools. Whom  is that Government here for? Actions
speak louder than words.
It is not just about policies; it is about the way the Government acts when it comes to
individuals who are in positions of wealth or  power. We have seen some examples in
recent weeks of this Government’s attitude  towards certain New Zealanders. We have
seen it with Judith Collins. We have seen it with Maurice Willia mson. In fact, we have
seen it from almost all of the Government members with their exclusive Cabinet clubs,
because what the Prime Mini ster did not acknowledge today when he tried to bandy
around that these were just simply innocuous forms of fund-raising is that the people
who belong to these clubs are not told they ar e part of a fund-raiser ; they are told they
are part of a club. They  are told they are part of a cl ub. A Government should never be
elected to serve for the exclusivity of the few or for the members of a club.
For the Labour Party, our driving force has always been very, very simple. Our ethos
has been simple. It has always been very cl ear. We have always been here because we
believe in serving on behalf of people. It is always what we have been about and we are
proud of that. I do not care if  the National Party members wa nt to mock us for having a
value set. I am proud of it—ever since Kirk wa s in this House and he simply articulated
it as all that people need is something to do, somewhere to live, someone to love, and
something to hope for. If you want to dis til down what we fight for every single day on
this side of the House, it is exactly that.
I have had from that side of the House questions over some of the policy ideas we
have raised. I am happy to outline all of th em. Starting in January was Best Start. Best
Start is a $600 million investment in childr en, acknowledging that if we want to move
forward as a nation, the best thing we can do  is invest in the early years of those
children by giving their parents choices, by ensuring that they have access to early
childhood education, and by increasing support fo r parents who need it most. That is
what that package was about and that is something we are really proud of.
Secondly, what about housing? That simple  issue of somewher e to live is not a
simple issue in New Zealand any more. It is increasingly unaffordable for families, and
particularly families with newborns are m oving more and more often. That impacts on
children’s education. That is why we have boldly said we will build 100,000 houses.
We will introduce a capital gains tax. We w ill introduce monetary policy that is focused
on families, interest rates, and employment. That is why we have boldly said we do not
care if we are having to be world leaders in  monetary policy if it means doing things on
behalf of people and putting people first in a market economy.
We have always been proud of our histor y. We are proud of our ideas because they
are positive. They are about focusing on what matters most. It is not about a club. It will
always be about people.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: Next Thursday our Minister of
Finance, the Hon Bill English, will be pres enting his sixth Budget, and, like our newly
minted Minister, Nicky Wa gner—congratulations—I have  a good feeling about this
7 May 2014 General Debate 17583
Budget. Already we have seen some good in itiatives coming through, and that is only
the start of what is to come.
For my part, I would like to concentrate in this call on what this John Key National-
led Government is doing for senior citizen s in New Zealand, the people who are very
vulnerable at the last stages of their lives. This year, for example, we are going to invest
more than $1.55 billion in aged  care. This is an increase  of over 60 percent under
Labour—$1.55 billion. So we are spending more on respite care, carer support, day
programmes for older people, and a lot of ot her initiatives that really will make a
difference to the quality of life of our seniors.
One example is that we have developed a new clinical asse ssment tool for aged care
providers. This ensures that each resident  in residential care will get up to two
nationally consistent clinical assessment te sts twice a year, or mo re if their health
suffers. That is the kind of thing that rea lly is important because older people’s health
does change quite dramatically and quite suddenly, so that is an important initiative, as
is, in this space, a national minimum standard, which will mean the same level of care is
going to be expected from providers ac ross New Zealand. Again, this is a very
important initiative, and we have tightened up on a lot of the regulations around
residential care. Across the boa rd, across this country, in ev ery electorate, and in every
home, you can relax in the knowledge that Ne w Zealand seniors are going to be better
looked after.
Elder abuse, in my opinion, has been a shameful secret for far too long, and this John
Key National-led Government is very committed to confronting elder abuse. We are
actively encouraging police to work more closely with partner organisations such as
Age Concern, which already does a very good job, but there is not  enough sharing of
information. There are too many silos around this kind of thing, so we are breaking
those down. We want to improve the responses to elder abuse.
The new Crimes Amendment Act, for example, which came into effect in 2012,
makes it an offence, with a maximum pena lty of 10 years in pr ison, to not take
reasonable steps to protect a child or a vulne rable adult. We are focusing on older New
Zealanders’ health and well-being. In my own North Shore electorate I have seen plenty
of examples of that. We have invested in  the past few years more than $200 million in
new facilities and new services. Gone are the dark days under Labour’s incompetent
Minister of Health Annette  King, when we saw long wai ting lists, people going to
Australia for cancer treatment, and just horrific situations—terrible situations. But under
the Hon Tony Ryall that has all changed.
In North Shore Hospital, for example, we have  just put in a state- of-the-art elective
surgery centre. We have a new emergenc y department and a new cardiology centre.
Last week I opened up a $3.5 million community dialysis centre. This  is the sort of
thing that makes an enormous difference to people’s lives, and it is complemented by
the dialysis centre on the North Shore Hospital site, which the Minister of Health, Tony
Ryall, opened a couple of years ago. So there has been a lot of spending—some $200
million on that one example of one hospital—but it does not stop there.
There are indeed a lot of th ings happening in terms of superannuation. In just over 5
years of a National Government the marri ed rate of superannuation has gone up by
$183.88 a fortnight and the single living al one payment has increased by $125.10 a
fortnight. That equates to a 25 percent increa se since April 2008. We stick with a plan.
We make one, we stick with it, and we stick with our promises. Our Prime Minister,
John Key, has undertaken to the people of New Zealand that we will maintain the
married rate of superannuati on at 66 percent of the aver age wage, and under our watch
the age of eligibility will remain at 65.
17584 General Debate 7 May 2014
The SuperGold card started out with very , very humble beginni ngs, and now we see
that there are more than 10,000 outlets in New Zealand that are involved in SuperGold.
Businesses range from pharmacies and dentists to transport and utility services.
Denis O’Rourke : It’s not a National Government achievement. That’s a New
Zealand First achievement.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: So from extremely humble beginnings we have managed to
crank it up. It is also now across Austra lia as well, so New Zealand seniors can go
across to Australia and receive a range of commercial discounts that are the same as
those that Australian seniors receive. So since 2010 our Government has not just
mithered on about it an d sort of suggested it  and then left well alone, as one of the
members who was heckling before was indicating—he was trying to claim the credit for
it. We have invested $68.6 million in the Supe rGold card scheme, and next week in the
Budget we will see even more exciting initiatives that will mean a brighter future for
New Zealanders. Thank you.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: National Party members have just spent the last half an
hour or so trying to convince New Zealanders th at they are interested in the issues that
matter to them. Well, tonight in the House th ey are going to get a chance to vote for an
issue that matters to New Zealanders. They can choose to vote to extend paid parental
leave to 26 weeks. So the question is wh ether they will. Will they put their money
where their mouth is and deal with that issue, or will they do what they have been doing
for weeks now and filibuster to try to de lay the Parental Leave and Employment
Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill from having its vote in
Parliament tonight? I th ink that is the sort of issue th at New Zealanders are going to
judge this Government on.
National Party members would have us believ e that they want to do things that are
relevant to people, but we are going to see whether that is true when they debate tonight.
Are they going to spend a lot of time ta lking about the Electronic Transactions
(Contract Formation) Amendment Bill, a tiny  little bill that rea lly does not impact
anybody at all, or are they going to let the House get on and vote for extending paid
parental leave to 26 weeks? The Government  has a problem. It has got a problem. This
bill defeats the Government. The only thing that stands between families and 26 weeks’
paid parental leave is the Government, b ecause the majority of members in this
Parliament will vote for that. I thank all of t hose parties that really are dealing with the
issues that matter to people, because if fa milies can get 26 weeks’ paid parental leave
with their newborn babies, then that will make a huge difference to people’s lives. If we
can get the bonding and attachment right, which we know now from all the research and
evidence is so important for helping children develop well, then we will have a much
better future in this country. The only thing that stands between now and that future is
the Government. So we will get to see toni ght whether those members are going to do
that. They have gone very quiet.
Government members say that they are going to deal with the issues that matter to
people. Well, what I want to know is which people. Are they the people who are in the
Cabinet club? Are those the people they are talking about? I believe they are. Someone
sent me a tweet today that I think said it all. They said: “Sue, do you know what a
‘Cabinet club’ handshake looks like? Of course you don’t, because it’s done in very
deep pockets, and you don’t get to see it.” That Cabinet club  handshake is done in very
deep pockets and with people who have the money to buy influence. That has been the
theme of the last week.
While we have been addressing issues that matter, like extending paid parental leave,
the Prime Minister has been spending his tim e trying to defend all of his colleagues and
7 May 2014 General Debate 17585
all of his Ministers from being donkey deep and dealin g with people who have the
money to buy influence. So—[Interruption]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry to
interrupt the honourable member, but I just re mind members that when we are having a
debate, people may interject on the speaker, but they cannot interject on each other if
they do not have the floor. It is very discourteous.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Thank you. I have obviously touche d a nerve there. What is the
theme here? Judith Collins was working with Oravida, with people who have the money
to buy influence. Maurice Williamson went and phoned the police to defend somebody
who has the money to buy influence. Then we  find out that they are all doing it—all of
the Ministers are involved in these Cabinet clubs.
I would like to know from the members opposite—could the next person who gets up
and speaks for the Government please tell us all of the electorates where these Cabinet
clubs operate. Where are the electorates wh ere these Cabinet clubs operate? Well,
maybe in 5 minutes you are not going to have ti me to list them all. Maybe it is going to
be quicker to name the electorates wher e there are no Cabinet clubs in operation,
because I think this is happening up and dow n the country. In every electorate, I am
guessing, there are going to be these people who belong to these exclusive clubs. They
pay money to belong to these exclusive cl ubs for one reason and one reason alone, and
that is to buy influence with Ministers in  the National Government. I want the members
opposite to name any of the electorates held  by their MPs that do not have a Cabinet
club. I think that will—well, Tau says he has not got one. There is one member who is
going to be honest about it.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s full
name.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Oh, Tau Henare—the Hon Tau He nare says he has not got a
Cabinet club, but he is  on his way out anyway. I want to  know from each one of those
members opposite which one of them has a Ca binet club, who is in that Cabinet club,
and what influence people are buying when they join up to the Cabinet club. I think that
those are the issues that we need to hear about before we see the Government’s Budget.

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: Kia ora mai an ō tātou katoa. Way back on
14 September 1972 a petition with more than 30,000 signatures was presented to
Parliament, spearheaded by the Te Reo M āori Society and Ng ā Tamatoa, calling for Te
Reo Māori to be taught in schools. That petition led directly to the creation of Te Tau o
te Reo M āori—which later became Te Wiki o Te Reo M āori—and to M āori being
included in the school curriculum. That love for the language  also led to the
establishment of the world-leading initiative to teach M āori to preschool children that is
the kōhanga reo movement. From k ōhanga we got kura kaupap a, and from kura we got
wharekura, and eventually we saw the establishment of Te W ānanga o Raukawa, Te
Wānanga o Aotearoa, and Te Whare Wānanga o Awanuiārangi.
In fact, the 1980s was a big time for Te Reo M āori. The M āori language claim was
lodged with the Waitangi Tribunal in  1985 by Huirangi Waikerepuru and Ng ā
Kaiwhakapūmau i Te Reo Māori, which sought official recognition for Te Reo Māori in
places as diverse as the courts, Government departments, local authorities, and even
Parliament itself, and for the Reo to be ma de compulsory in schools, a claim widely
supported by all corners of the M āori world. The tribunal ru led that the Crown had
failed to protect the M āori language and recommended that Te Reo M āori be legally
recognised as an official language, that a st atutory body be established to foster the use
of Te Reo M āori, and that a broadcasting policy be  formulated to help promote the
language. In 1987 the M āori Language Act was passed, making M āori an official
17586 General Debate 7 May 2014
language, and Te Taura Whiri i te Reo M āori was established to promote the use of Te
Reo Māori as a living language.
Those initiatives were further enhanced  by another claim led by Huirangi
Waikerepuru and Ng ā Kaiwhakap ūmau i Te Reo M āori, stating that the M āori
Language Act had failed to address radio and television broadcasting, and a claim from
Sir Graham Latimer and the New Zealand M āori Council calling on the Crown to
recognise Māori interests in the radio spectrum.  The Crown opposed both claims, and
Māori were forced to take their case to the High Court, the Court of Appeal, and
ultimately to the Privy Council, where they won support for an amendment to the
Broadcasting Act in 1993 to establish Te M āngai P āho to fund M āori language
television and radio program mes under the Minister at the time, the Hon Maurice
Williamson. Today we have 21 M āori radio stations around the country, and M āori
Television finally went to air on 28 March 2004 . But in case anyone thinks that things
are all OK with the Reo now, please note that  just 2 years ago the Waitangi Tribunal
ruled that the Government had breached th e Treaty of Waitangi by systemically failing
to fund and support the k ōhanga reo M āori language strategy, that the Government
should apologise for its failings, and that it should appoint an independent adviser to
oversee an urgent programme to overhaul policy, increase participation, improve
quality, increase funding, and provide th e support necessary for the upgrade and
maintenance of kōhanga facilities.
That is just a snapshot of the last 40 years of the struggle that M āori have been
through to get Te Reo M āori recognised and to get resources committed to keeping it
alive. In all of that, it is  worth noting that th e struggle was led by those who cared for
the Reo, those who had a deep and abiding love  for the Reo, and that they often did so
at great personal cost to themselves and their families. Many of those early pioneers
either could not even speak Te Reo or were themselves just taking their first tentative
steps along the pathway of Māori language revitalisation. They were often castigated by
older, more conservative native M āori language speakers for daring to lead the charge
for the Reo. But their passion and their commitment and their refusal to take a backward
step marked them out as true champions for the language.
And that is the reason Mana opposes the Government’s plan to take the language
away from those who care for it and to give  it to those who woul d corporatise it. The
plan, led by the M āori Party, is to scrap Te Taura Whiri i te Reo M āori and Te M āngai
Pāho and to put the language into the hands of corporate iwi leaders. We oppose its plan
because the grim reality is that iwi leader s at that level are simply not capable of
managing such a taonga. They were not there when the people needed them to lead the
fight for the Reo. Their corporate statements  speak glowingly of the importance of the
Reo but their financial statements suggest that they have other priorities.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): We have been hearing a lot from the
Opposition members today around Cabinet club s and their great concern about what
might somewhat transparently be happening in  the Government over here. Well, I have
been fascinated, as they have talked about  money and influence and access, to think
about what is the world’s largest Cabine t club. Ladies and ge ntlemen, the largest
Cabinet club of money and in fluence and access is the unions—the unions that behold
that crowd opposite every day. Do you know what makes it worse? Do you know what
makes it even worse? The constitution and structure of the New Zealand Labour Party
allow the unions—the unions of New Zealan d—to decide who the Labour Party leader
is, and, God forbid, who could be a Labour Prime Minister. That is buying access.
Do you know what makes it even worse? Even worse is that the unions are taking the
money from the pockets of hard-working Ne w Zealanders, particularly in the Civil
Service. I remember it well. They take money from hard-working Kiwis, push it on to
7 May 2014 General Debate 17587
their union hacks, and then pass it on to the hacks who sit on the other side of this
House. [Interruption]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am very reluctant to
interrupt a member who is in  a 5-minute speaking slot, so I am going to allow him to
start again. I am going to allow him to start again because I have two members who do
not have the floor who c ontinue to interject on e ach other. It is tota lly out of order. The
member can start again.
SIMON O’CONNOR: I will not continue on this line of vitriol per se, but I think
the reminder is there: if the party opposite wants to talk about money and it wants to
talk about access and it wants to talk about influence, then it must begin and end with a
conversation about the Labour Party and the ro le of the unions. I go back to that other
point that it is money taken from hard-wor king, ordinary Kiwis, channelled through the
system. Once again, you see it in the cons titution of the Labour Party, which gives
effective majority control to the unions to decide the leadership. That is just shocking.
I am looking forward to this Government’s  sixth Budget. The fine electorate of
Tāmaki is looking forward—

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Magnificent.
SIMON O’CONNOR : —the magnificent electorate of T āmaki, thank you to the
member.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Almost as good as the North Shore beaches.
SIMON O’CONNOR: Almost as good as the North Shore. And why are we looking
forward to it? Because we are a positive pa rty looking for a bright er future. We know
that we sit on great news, like 3 percent growth. Some economists are forecasting even
higher. We know that over 1,500 people a week  are coming off welfare. Unlike the
other side, who are a lot of sort of theoreti cians, those of us who have worked on the
front line—in fact, within the likes of Work and Income—know that for those 1,500
individuals, going into work changes their liv es. This Government is committed to that.
To the Labour Party that is just a number and something to be heckled at, but, again, for
the real, hard-working, expe rienced people on this side of the House it makes a
difference. There were 84,000 more jobs adde d to the economy in the last 12 months.
Unemployment is at 6 percent and it is forecast  to go even lower. Contrast that with the
OECD rate of 7.6 percent. We are on our wa y to surplus. This National Government
promised it, and we will deliver it.
What about the other side, though? What about the other side? They are completely
distracted, never focused on the issues that matter. All we heard was rambling rhetoric. I
think there was a promise of unicorns, fluffy bunnies, and rainbows in there somewhere.
In fact, when Opposition members even come to  try to do a policy, it really is sort of
being akin to a theomachist in an apotheca ry. Most people will not know what that
means, and that is a good analogy because no one understands what Labour’s policies
mean.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Or care less.
SIMON O’CONNOR : Or care less. Well, actually, I quite like the word
“apothecary”.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: What policies?
SIMON O’CONNOR: What policies? It is a shocker. What we do know is that there
would be higher taxes from Labour and the Greens and more taxes through their
emission trading scheme. Have no illusion, New Zealand, things like the emission
trading scheme, capital gains taxes, and ch anges to KiwiSaver are costs to you. They
want to nationalise the electricity system. I heard the other day that I think the Greens in
particular now are against milk products and logs. What are we left with in this country?
They really also want to spend like troope rs. Well, we are a prudent Government. We
17588 General Debate 7 May 2014
are a prudent Government. We have capped it,  effectively, at up to $1 billion of new
spending because we know that that is the prudent and right thing to do. The majority of
Kiwis understand this, and that is why the La bour Party and its union mates are polling
under 30 percent—

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: And down—going down.
SIMON O’CONNOR : —and continuing to go down. That is why a certain Mr
Jones jumped.
But what about the wins? We are seeing some prefigurations—[ Interruption] Or he
was pushed, as my honourable colleague notes.  We are looking at some really serious
positive wins for Kiwis at the moment, like $6.3 million over 4 years for bilateral
cochlear implants. As someone who has worked with them—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: How much, sorry?
SIMON O’CONNOR : $6.3 million. As someone who has worked in the health
system, what a difference that makes. I would like to suggest, though we probably
cannot find the money, that we probably need some implants for the Opposition
members so they can truly hear the wants of New Zealanders. We heard from Paula
Bennett that there is $10.4 million in new operating funding to support sexual violence
services. That is absolutely critical, abso lutely important. As someone who has worked
in the community for years—an d I think, particularly, of wo rking as a chaplain at Mt
Eden prison—and seen the abuse and the violence that happen to our most vulnerable, it
is critical to get in early to make a real difference.
As I turn towards the end, because I am c onscious of time, I want to turn to T āmaki.
There are many, many local wins that this G overnment has delivered to the people of
Tāmaki—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: And continuing to deliver.
SIMON O’CONNOR : —and it will continue to do so, like $3 million to the St
Thomas School for new buildings, and ultra-fast broadband to our schools. We have the
Tāmaki Transformation Programme, an agreement between the Government and the
council, working with the Auckland cham ber of commerce, around a Career Start
programme. The Career Start programme is a cooperation of the T āmaki
Transformation Programme, the Government, and the council to help young people into
jobs. There is new housing in Glen Innes and Panmure and the electrification of rail.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
